---
title: "Calling the emulator"
---

Getting a trajectory out of stateMINT takes two calls, one to fetch a checkpoint from Hugging
Face and one to run it over a list of scenarios.

## Loading a checkpoint

```{python}
from stateMINT.model import Mamba2Regressor

prevalence = Mamba2Regressor.from_pretrained(
    "dide-ic/stateMINT", predictor="prevalence", revision="v1.2.2",
)

print(type(prevalence).__name__)
print(prevalence.model_config["predictor"])
```

::: {.callout-note}
## The return type

The classmethod hangs off `Mamba2Regressor`, but what it hands back is a `ModelArtifact`, a
container holding the network (`.model`), its architecture (`.model_config`), the input recipe
(`.preprocessing_config`) and the fitted covariate scaler (`.scaler`). You call `.predict` on the
artifact, not the network.
:::

`predictor` selects which of the two checkpoints to fetch. The two are separately trained
networks carrying separately fitted scalers, and the scalers are not interchangeable.

```{python}
import numpy as np

cases = Mamba2Regressor.from_pretrained(
    "dide-ic/stateMINT", predictor="cases", revision="v1.2.2",
)

print("same scaler means:", np.allclose(prevalence.scaler.mean_, cases.scaler.mean_))
```

Load the artifact that matches the quantity you want. Both take the same twelve inputs and return
the same shape, so reading a prevalence prediction as case counts raises no error. It returns a
wrong answer, scaled for the other target.

## Predicting

`.predict` takes a list of dicts, one per scenario, and returns a `(B, 157)` array, one row per
scenario and one column per fortnightly window.

```{python}
district = {
    "eir": 31.96,          # from estiMINT, for a measured prevalence of 0.45
    "dn0_use": 0.311,      # pyrethroid-only nets at 30% resistance
    "Q0": 0.85,
    "phi_bednets": 0.80,
    "seasonal": 0,
    "routine": 0.0,
    "itn_use": 0.70,
    "irs_use": 0.0,
    "dn0_future": 0.485,   # switch to PBO
    "itn_future": 0.70,    # same coverage sustained
    "irs_future": 0.0,
    "lsm": 0.0,
}

y = prevalence.predict([district])
print(y.shape)
print(f"prevalence at the campaign: {y[0, 78]:.3f}")
```

Column 78 is the window the campaign lands in, and the value there sits close to the 0.45 given
to estiMINT. [Covariates and the time grid](covariates.qmd) derives that index from the checkpoint
rather than assuming it. Scenarios come back stacked, in the order you supplied them.

```{python}
campaigns = [
    dict(district, dn0_future=0.0,   itn_future=0.0),   # nets withdrawn
    dict(district, dn0_future=0.311, itn_future=0.70),  # like-for-like pyrethroid
    dict(district, dn0_future=0.485, itn_future=0.70),  # switch to PBO
]

Y = prevalence.predict(campaigns)
print(Y.shape)
print(np.round(Y[:, -1], 3))   # prevalence three years on
```

## Transformed space

The networks are trained on transformed targets, a logit for prevalence and a `log1p` for cases.
`.predict` inverts the transform by default. `transformed=True` suppresses the inversion. You want
that only when scoring the network against a held-out set in its training space.

```{python}
raw = prevalence.predict([district], transformed=True)
inv = prevalence.predict([district])

print("logit space  :", np.round(raw[0, :3], 3))
print("prevalence   :", np.round(inv[0, :3], 3))
print("sigmoid(raw) :", np.round(1 / (1 + np.exp(-raw[0, :3])), 3))
```

## Negative case counts

The inverse of `log1p` is `expm1`, so a prediction slightly below zero in log space becomes a case
count slightly below zero, by a fraction of a case. Under a strong campaign, where true incidence
is close to the floor, it happens often.

```{python}
aggressive = dict(
    district, dn0_future=0.55, itn_future=0.95, irs_future=0.90, lsm=0.90,
)

c = cases.predict([aggressive])
print(f"minimum        : {c.min():.4f}")
print(f"negative steps : {int((c < 0).sum())} of {c.shape[1]}")

c = np.maximum(c, 0.0)
print(f"after flooring : {c.min():.4f}")
```

Floor the case trajectory with `np.maximum` before you plot it or sum it.
[`run_scenarios`](../06-scenarios/run-scenarios.qmd) applies exactly this floor, so only results
taken straight from a checkpoint need it.

Prevalence needs no such treatment. A logit inverts through a sigmoid, and a sigmoid cannot leave
`[0, 1]`.

## The raw feature matrix

`.prepare_inputs` runs the first half of `.predict` and stops. It expands the twelve covariates
onto the time grid, masks the campaign fields before day 3285, scales everything and appends the
time features.

```{python}
X = prevalence.prepare_inputs(campaigns)
print(X.shape, X.dtype)
```

The sixteen channels are the twelve scaled covariates plus four time features locating each window
in the year and relative to the campaign. The order of the channels is set out in
[stateMINT internals](../07-under-the-hood/statemint-internals.qmd).

## Pinning the revision

`revision` is optional and defaults to `main`, which moves, so an unpinned analysis may not re-run
on the weights it ran today. The published tags run from `v1.0.0` to `v1.2.2`. Pass one explicitly.

```python
Mamba2Regressor.from_pretrained("dide-ic/stateMINT", predictor="cases", revision="v1.2.2")
```

## See also

The 157 columns go onto a real time axis in [Plotting trajectories](plotting.qmd). Fifty scenarios
in one call are far cheaper than fifty calls of one, and [Performance and caching](performance.qmd)
has the timings and the cache settings.
